accuracy.where: ## Your half of the interview, "Spot the questions talking can't settle" bullet: "The prototype gets its own folder and a fresh session." (line 166)
accuracy.problem: The Lesson says the prototype gets its own folder. The prototype Skill and the Prototype Lesson both say otherwise. The Skill puts prototype code next to the code it is for, inside the same project. The Prototype Lesson runs the fresh session in the same project folder and justifies `/handoff` as a side task forked off mid-work, not as a move to a new folder. A Visitor following this Lesson would make a new folder, which the other Lesson tells them not to do. The sentence order also puts `/prototype` before the `/handoff` that has to come first.
accuracy.evidence: ~/.claude/plugins/cache/claude-plugins-official/mattpocock-skills/1.3.1/skills/engineering/prototype/SKILL.md:20: "Locate the prototype code close to where it will actually be used (next to the module or page it's prototyping for)". content/lessons/06-prototype.md:157: "The fresh session is just `claude` started in a second terminal window while the first stays open"; 06-prototype.md:187: `/handoff` only if something must travel, here "a side task forked off mid-work"; 06-prototype.md:270: the Try it round trip runs `cd book-loans`, the same folder. Only ask-matt/SKILL.md:20 says "a prototype lives in its own directory", so the Skill files disagree with each other. The Lesson should follow the prototype Skill and the Prototype Lesson.
accuracy.fix: Replace "The prototype gets its own folder and a fresh session. To carry your decisions there, type `/handoff`, a Skill that writes what matters into a file the new session can read. Once you've seen the answer, type `/handoff` again to bring it back." with "First type `/handoff`, a Skill that writes what matters into a file a new session can read. Then start a fresh session in a second terminal window, so the prototype's tokens stay out of your interview, and build it there. Once you've seen the answer, type `/handoff` again to bring it back."

accuracy.problem: The sources don't support the session-length range the Lesson gives. The AI Hero docs' examples run from three questions to fifty, plus a two-hundred-question session given as the over-scoped case. Thirteen and forty-six are only two examples from the middle of that range. The spot-passive feedback states it as a ceiling ("up to forty-six"), which the docs contradict.

What went wrong?"
accuracy.fix: Line 61: "How long does that take? It varies: Matt's docs on AI Hero (his teaching site) say some plans need three questions and some need fifty, and his own sessions usually run to about twenty." Line 384 feedback: "Session length varies a lot; Matt's docs say some plans need fifty questions."

accuracy.where: ## The idea, rule 2: "It isn't over until the frontier is empty and you say so." (line 59), against line 61: "There's no limit; to stop early, say "let's wrap up"." and Try it step 7 (line 252)
accuracy.problem: Rule 2 says the session can't end before the frontier is empty. Two lines later the Lesson says you can stop early, and the Try it has the Visitor do exactly that after two or three rounds. A cold reader gets two rules that clash. The Skill defines "done" as an empty frontier, and the docs add that you can tell it to wrap up and accept the plan where it stands. The confirmation gate holds either way.
accuracy.evidence: grilling/SKILL.md:30: "The session is done when the frontier is empty"; https://www.aihero.dev/skills-grilling: "Tell it to wrap up, or stop and accept the plan where it stands."
accuracy.fix: Line 61: replace "There's no limit; to stop early, say "let's wrap up"." with "There's no cap. To stop before the frontier is empty, say "let's wrap up": it summarises where things stand and still waits for your yes."

quiz.where: Checkpoint who-can-start (Which grilling Skill to type), line 119: "`/grilling`, because it's model-invoked."
quiz.problem: The right option gives the answer away. The prompt asks which Skill the agent can load "on its own", and line 96 defines a model-invoked Skill as one the agent can pick up "on its own". So the option's reason just restates the prompt's condition in the Lesson's own term. The two distractors give reasons that aren't about who can start the Skill ("the request asks for a grilling", "you're in a repo"). A reader who can't remember which of the three Skills is model-invoked still picks c just by matching the term to the prompt. Telling the three apart is the one thing this Checkpoint is meant to check.
quiz.evidence: Line 114: "Which Skill can the agent load on its own?" Line 96: "Others, model-invoked Skills, can also be picked up by the agent on its own". Line 115: "`/grill-me`, because the request asks for a grilling." Line 117: "`/grill-with-docs`, because you're in a repo." The classification itself is right: grill-me/SKILL.md:4 and grill-with-docs/SKILL.md:4 have `disable-model-invocation: true`, and grilling/SKILL.md has no such line.
quiz.fix: Remove the reasons from all three options and put the reasoning in the feedback. Order and [x] stay the same. a: "- [ ] `/grill-me`" with feedback "> `/grill-me` is user-invoked, so it only starts when you type its name. Asking for a grilling in plain words isn't enough." b: "- [ ] `/grill-with-docs`" with feedback "> Also user-invoked. The agent can't start it for you, even in a repo." c: "- [x] `/grilling`" with feedback "> Right. `/grilling` is model-invoked: the one member of the family the agent may load on its own when your words match its description." Rendered lengths are 9/16/9, so the right answer isn't the longest.

quiz.where: Checkpoint steer-details (Your half of the interview), prompt line 173 "CSS class names, file names and folder layout" and right option line 180 "Tell it to decide those details itself, using best practice."
quiz.problem: This tests recognition, not transfer. The prompt reuses the worked Scene's own details (CSS and file names), and the right option repeats the Scene's and the Site story's wording ("decide … using best practice") almost word for word. A reader can match the phrase without understanding the idea. The writing guide says to use a fresh situation and not to repeat the body's example.
quiz.evidence: Line 142 (Scene): "don't ask me about CSS or file names: decide those yourself using best practice." Line 164: "where you handed over CSS (the code that styles a page) and file names." Line 286 (Site story): "decide the details itself using best practice". Writing guide line 118: "Use a fresh situation … not the body's own example sentence."
quiz.fix: Prompt: "You're grilling a plant-swap site. Two rounds in, most questions have been about button colours, fonts and what to name each page's file. You only care about who can list plants and what's left out of v1. What do you do?" Option d: "Say which parts you care about and let it settle the rest." (58 characters; a is 64). Feedback d: "> Right. You own the scope; the agent owns the details. Tell it which branches matter to you and to decide the rest itself, and the rounds go there."

quiz.where: Final test scenario-overwhelmed, prompt line 358: "Round 1 arrives with eight questions and you freeze. What's the supported way to get smaller rounds from now on?"
quiz.problem: The prompt replays the Site story (round 1 had 8 questions and it overwhelmed the author). It also uses the body's own phrase for the answer, "the supported way to get smaller". A reader who remembers the word "supported" from the sentence that introduces the CLAUDE.md line can find the answer without understanding why rounds are big or what CLAUDE.md does.
quiz.evidence: Line 284 (Site story): "Round 1 had 8 questions, and it overwhelmed me … the `CLAUDE.md` line above is the supported way to get smaller ones." Line 170: "there's a supported opt-out."
quiz.fix: Prompt: "Grilling a plant-swap site, round 1 brings nine questions at once and you lose track halfway. You want every grilling session from now on to give you less at a time. What do you do?" Options, order and feedback stay as they are. Option b's feedback can still call the line "the documented opt-out".

quiz.where: Final test scenario-overwhelmed, option c feedback, line 364: "Plan mode pushes the agent to rush to a plan. It doesn't change how grilling asks."
quiz.problem: The second sentence contradicts the Lesson and Matt's docs. Both say plan mode does change how grilling asks: the agent stops questioning sooner and rushes to a plan. A reader who has just read "instead of asking" is told the opposite here.
quiz.evidence: Line 168: "Plan mode … rushes the agent to that plan instead of asking." Line 179: "Plan mode pushes the agent to rush to a plan instead of interviewing you." https://www.aihero.dev/skills-grill-me (fetched 2026-10-24) says to keep plan mode off: "Plan mode makes the agent hurry to produce a plan".
quiz.fix: Feedback c: "> Plan mode makes the agent hurry to a plan and ask less, not ask in smaller rounds."

quiz.problem: There's a wording tell that a test-wise reader can use across the spot- questions. The wrong options are written as fixes ("X should …"), and the right option is the only plain statement of what went wrong. In spot-passive both wrong options are "should" sentences. In spot-asked-for-fact both wrong options start "It should" and the right one starts "It asks". In spot-cleared-early two of the three wrong options are "should have" sentences. Picking the option that isn't a "should" sentence gets all three right.
quiz.evidence: spot-passive: a "…grilling should take ten minutes at most.", b "Lee should have answered each question in a separate message.", right c "Lee never pushed back, so the decisions were the agent's." spot-asked-for-fact: right a "It asks you for a fact…", b "It should wait for round 2…", c "It should be multiple choice…". spot-cleared-early: a "`/to-spec` should have run before…", d "She should have answered every single question…", right b "`/clear` emptied out…".
quiz.fix: Reword the distractors as statements of what went wrong, keeping their meaning, order and feedback. spot-passive a: "The session ran too long: an hour is more than grilling needs." b: "Answering whole rounds in one reply rushed Lee's choices." spot-asked-for-fact b: "It's too detailed for round 1, which is only for big decisions." c: "It offers one guess instead of listing every language it might be." spot-cleared-early a: "`/to-spec` ran too late; it belonged before the grilling." d: "Splitting the questions into rounds scattered her answers." None of these makes a right answer the longest (checked: 62/57/57, 48/63/66, 55/54/48/58).

quiz.where: Final test spot-asked-for-fact, prompt line 392: "During a grilling session the agent asks: "❓ Q2 - Language: Is your site's code written in TypeScript?…""
quiz.problem: The prompt never says the code already exists. This course's readers start in empty folders (the Try it does), and for a site that isn't built yet, the language is a decision, not a fact. A sharp reader could then reject the key's claim that the agent should look it up.
quiz.evidence: Line 58: a fact is something "it could look up (like which database the project already uses)". grilling/SKILL.md:28: facts are things "from the environment (filesystem, tools, etc.)". Line 229: the Try it starts with an empty folder.
quiz.fix: Prompt: "Grilling a change in your site's repo, which already has code, the agent asks: "❓ Q2 - Language: Is the site's code written in TypeScript? ➡️ Yes, probably." What's wrong with this question?"

quiz.where: Checkpoint frontier-wait, right option line 84: "Until voting is settled, the vote count may never matter."
quiz.problem: The right option is the only hedged one ("may never"). The three distractors all state something flatly. Hedging is a known tell for the right answer.
quiz.evidence: Lines 86, 88, 90: "The agent asks the easy questions first…", "Each round is capped at three questions.", "It's a fact, so the agent will look it up…"
quiz.fix: Option a: "It only matters if members vote, and that isn't settled yet." (60 characters; b is 78). The feedback stays.

quiz.problem: The prompt copies the Scene's closing summary word for word, and it clashes with the Scene, where "you" answered "2 yes" to permanent comments. A reader may stop to wonder why they'd now want editing, when the point is just to practise correcting a summary. The guide asks for a fresh situation.
quiz.evidence: Line 144: "Anonymous comments, optional name, permanent, newest first. Out of scope: login, editing, moderation. Is that our shared understanding?" is repeated at line 148. Line 136: "1 yes, 2 yes, 3 no…", where Q2 at line 133 is "Should comments be permanent once posted?"
quiz.fix: Prompt: "Grilling a plant-swap site, the agent ends: "Swaps arranged by message, listings expire after 30 days. Out of scope: payments, delivery, ratings. Is that our shared understanding?" You actually wanted members to rate a swap afterwards. What do you do?" Option a: "Say yes for now, and ask for ratings once the code has been written." Option c: "Start a separate grilling session just about ratings." b's feedback: "…Ratings can raise new questions (who can rate whom? can a rating change?), so answer that round, then say yes." Order and [x] stay the same.

quiz.where: Final test sequence-multi-session, prompt line 414: "planning a feature that will take several sessions"
quiz.problem: The prompt doesn't make the split the Lesson teaches: whether you can plan the work in one sitting, not whether building it takes one session. ask-matt's own wording ("a huge feature build, too big for one session") sends that case to `/wayfinder`, so a reader who knows that may hesitate. No option offers `/wayfinder`, so the key still stands, but the prompt should match the table.
quiz.evidence: Line 108: "any change you can plan in one sitting, even if building it takes several sessions | `/grill-with-docs`". ask-matt/SKILL.md:52: "A huge, foggy effort: a greenfield project or a huge feature build, too big for one session → `/wayfinder`". Writing guide line 113 states the plan-vs-build split.
quiz.fix: Prompt: "You're in a repo, planning a feature you can talk through in one sitting but that will take several sessions to build. Which order is right?"

reader.where: ## Your half of the interview, ""I don't know" is a real answer too: a question you can't answer is often one to prototype rather than guess." (line 163); also "Start in a fresh conversation, not on top of a plan the agent already wrote." (line 168)
reader.problem: Both sentences are near-verbatim copies of sentences on Matt's AI Hero /grill-me page, with no quotation marks. That page's one allowed quote is already used at line 161 ("It's a conversation, not an interview."). Line 163 keeps about 18 of its 21 words in the source's order.
reader.evidence: https://www.aihero.dev/skills-grill-me (updated 2026-08-24), Common questions, says: 'Say so. "I don't know" is a real answer, and a question you can't answer is usually a sign to prototype rather than to guess.' Its 'When to reach for it' section says: 'Start it in a fresh conversation, not on top of a plan you already had an agent write.' Line 161 of the Lesson already quotes the same page. The task rules allow at most one quote per source; everything else must be in the author's own words.
reader.fix: Line 163: replace the sentence with: 'Saying "I don't know" is fine too. Often it means you need to see a prototype before you can decide.' Line 168: replace the last sentence with: 'And begin the grilling in a new conversation, before the agent has drafted any plan of its own.'

reader.where: ## Your half of the interview, "To carry your decisions there, type `/handoff`, a Skill that writes what matters into a file the new session can read. Once you've seen the answer, type `/handoff` again to bring it back." (line 166)
reader.problem: A reader would expect `/handoff` to move the decisions by itself, both into the prototype session and back. In fact it only writes a file to the OS temp folder. You have to point the new session at that file, then hand the second file to your original grilling session. The bullet's fallback, 'if that doesn't start Matt's Skill', also gives the reader no sign to watch for. The Prototype Lesson names the symptom: "unknown skill".
reader.evidence: handoff/SKILL.md:8: 'Save to the temporary directory of the user's OS ($TMPDIR, else /tmp; %TEMP% on Windows) - not the current workspace.' ask-matt/SKILL.md:21-23: '/handoff out, then open a fresh session against that file' ... '/handoff back what you learned, and reference it from the original idea thread.' content/lessons/06-prototype.md:47: 'if `/prototype` says "unknown skill", type `/mattpocock-skills:prototype` instead.'
reader.fix: Replace from 'Detour through' to the end of the bullet with: 'Detour through a quick throwaway build with `/prototype` (if it says "unknown skill", type `/mattpocock-skills:prototype`). The prototype gets its own folder and a fresh session: `/handoff` writes your decisions to a file and says where, and you ask the new session to read it. A second `/handoff` there writes the answer, which you give back to this session. [Prototype](/learn/prototype) shows each step.'

reader.where: ## Your half of the interview, "(it lives at `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`, where `~` is your home folder; create it if it doesn't exist)" (line 170)
reader.problem: A Visitor who barely uses a terminal has no way to create a file in the hidden `.claude` folder. Windows File Explorer has no `~` either. Yet this is the opt-out the scenario-overwhelmed Final test question asks about. Claude Code has a Built-in command, `/memory`, that creates the file for you, and the How coding agents work Lesson already teaches it (01-how-agents-work.md:196).
reader.evidence: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory: '/memory lists your CLAUDE.md ... including user and project CLAUDE.md entries for files that don't exist yet ... selecting one that doesn't exist yet creates it first.' The same page also says: 'ask Claude directly, like "add this to CLAUDE.md"'.
reader.fix: Replace the parenthesis with: '(it lives in your home folder, at `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`. The easy way: type `/memory`, a Built-in command, and pick the user file, which is created if it doesn't exist; or ask Claude Code to add the line to your global CLAUDE.md)'. In Common mistakes (line 270), write 'a line in that same global `CLAUDE.md`'.

GLOSSARY.md:58: the Site story is 'kept apart from the teaching'.

You want smaller rounds in every grilling session from now on, not just this one. What should you do?' Cut the Site story parenthetical at line 284, or shorten it to '(Big rounds are normal.)'.

reader.where: ## The idea: a tree of decisions, asked in rounds, "A question that depends on another question still open in the same round belongs in a later round. The agent judges this, so if two answers in one round clash, say so and it reopens that branch." (line 54)
reader.problem: The first sentence keeps 14 of its 18 words in the order of the SKILL.md line it is based on, which breaks the rule against copying a 15+-word SKILL.md sentence. It also repeats the frontier definition from line 40. The second sentence's 'so' doesn't follow for a cold reader: why would two independent questions clash?
reader.evidence: grilling/SKILL.md:26: 'A question whose answer depends on another question still open in this round belongs to a _later_ round, not this one.' https://www.aihero.dev/skills-grilling: 'The agent chooses it by judgement; it does not compute it from a graph ... The only guard is to tell it. That reopens the affected branch in the next round.'
reader.fix: Replace both sentences with: 'The agent picks each round by judgement, so once in a while one of your answers changes another question from the same round. If you spot that, say so, and it reopens that branch next round.'

reader.where: The idea, rule 1: "Decisions, like "should comments be editable?", always come to you." (line 58), against the chat Scene "decide those yourself using best practice" (line 142) and "let it decide the rest" (line 164)
reader.problem: A cold reader learns as a firm rule that decisions always come to them, and that an agent answering its own decisions has broken the Skill. Then the Scene, the steering bullet and the steer-details right answer all tell them to let the agent decide things. The Lesson never joins the two ideas: handing a branch over is itself your decision. So the advice can look like it breaks rule 1.
reader.evidence: grilling/SKILL.md:28: "The _decisions_ are the user's: put each to them and wait." Lesson line 142: "decide those yourself using best practice". Line 164: "let it decide the rest". Checkpoint steer-details right option: "Hand those details to it and steer it to your priorities." Its feedback only explains "nothing silently assumed", not "always come to you".
reader.fix: End rule 1 with: "Decisions, like "should comments be editable?", always come to you, even if your answer is "you pick": handing a detail over is itself a decision."
